analysis.one_liner: Strips legal immunity from large social media sites whose algorithms amplify content that injures someone.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by the chairman of the committee that would handle it, never received a markup or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Section 230 of the Communications Act — the law that generally shields online platforms from lawsuits over what other people post — so that very large platforms lose that shield when a personalized algorithm they use pushes content that causes physical or severe emotional injury to someone. It would apply only to services with more than 5 million monthly visitors, and it would not touch search results people ask for directly, small sites, or the internet's infrastructure providers like web hosts and data storage. Injured users could then sue the biggest platforms when a platform knew or should have known its recommendations were contributing to harm.
analysis.who_benefits: People physically or emotionally injured by content that a large platform's algorithm amplified toward them — for example, material linked to self-harm, disordered eating, or targeted harassment — would gain a path to sue the platform in court. Small platforms and internet infrastructure companies also benefit from being explicitly left out of the new liability, keeping the protections they have today.

how_it_helps.text: Removes Section 230 liability protection for large platforms when a personalized recommendation materially contributes to a physical or severe emotional injury to any person.

Applies only where the platform knew or should have known it was making the personalized recommendation, or made it recklessly — a standard aimed at deliberate or indifferent conduct rather than ordinary moderation mistakes.
Targets the largest services — those with more than 5 million unique monthly visitors — so lawsuits would fall on companies with the resources to redesign algorithms, not on small sites and startups.

Exempts user-directed search results and internet infrastructure such as web hosting, domain registration, content delivery networks, caching, data storage, and cybersecurity, so lawsuits aimed at social media feeds cannot be redirected at the companies that keep the internet running.

analysis.who_pays: The largest social media companies would bear new litigation risk and the cost of changing or narrowing the algorithms that decide what content each user sees. They would likely respond by restricting or removing more content, including lawful speech, to avoid lawsuits, and the added legal exposure could concentrate the market further around firms able to absorb it.

drawbacks.text: Exposing platforms to lawsuits over recommendation algorithms could push them to over-remove lawful speech, since the safest response to litigation risk is to show users less.

The exemption for services with 5 million or fewer monthly visitors creates a bright line that spares small and mid-size platforms from the same liability, raising the argument that the rules would be uneven across the internet.
'Severe emotional injury' is a subjective standard, and the bill was never amended or tested in committee, so critics and supporters alike could not know how courts would apply it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real, narrow problem — large companies algorithmically amplifying content that injures people and being untouchable in court because of Section 230 — while leaving search, small sites, and infrastructure alone. Its knowing-or-reckless standard limits suits to the worst cases, but the emotional-injury standard and the litigation pressure on content moderation are genuine costs that a working version of the law would have had to balance in committee. It never got that chance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to its Communications and Technology subcommittee three days later, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on October 15, 2021 with Reps. Michael Doyle, Jan Schakowsky, and Anna Eshoo — all Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on October 18, 2021.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have carved Section 230 liability out only for large providers whose personalized recommendations knowingly or recklessly contributed to physical or severe emotional injury, exempting small services, user-directed search, and internet infrastructure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest social media platforms, which kept their Section 230 immunity for algorithmically recommended content and face no lawsuits over injuries tied to their recommendation systems.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee; took no further action to advance it.

for.name: Reps. Michael Doyle, Jan Schakowsky, and Anna Eshoo
for.role: Original cosponsors, all senior members of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; none advanced the bill further.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by the bill's sponsor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Communications and Technology subcommittee on October 18, 2021 and never held a markup or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee and no Republican cosponsored the bill; no opposition vote was ever recorded because it never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Large social media platforms (Meta, YouTube, TikTok-class services)
industries.note: The bill would strip their Section 230 immunity when personalized recommendations materially contribute to physical or severe emotional injury, exposing them to lawsuits. Because the bill died, their immunity for algorithmic amplification is untouched.

industries.industry: Internet infrastructure (web hosting, domain registration, CDNs, data storage, cybersecurity)
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts these providers, guaranteeing they keep full Section 230 protection even as the big consumer platforms lose it.
Services with 5 million or fewer monthly visitors are exempt from the new liability, sparing them litigation costs their larger competitors would face.
